By BRIAN MARKS, US ASSISTANT SHOWBUSINESS EDITOR and LILLIAN GISSEN, US DEPUTY LIFESTYLE EDITOR
Published: 21:48 EDT, 1 October 2026 | Updated: 23:26 EDT, 1 October 2026
Ken Urker, the former fiancé of convicted murderer Gypsy-Rose Blanchard, has died at the age of 33.
Urker was discovered unresponsive in Louisiana on Thursday, October 1, the same day that he was celebrating his birthday, TMZ reported.
Blanchard had reportedly texted Urker 'Happy Birthday,' but she never received a response.
Family sources told the publication that Urker – who shared a daughter with Blanchard – was discovered at home by her brother, Dylan.
According to People , Dylan and his wife had planned to go out to dinner with Urker before they arrived at his home.
They added that the tragic news had left both Blanchard and Urker's families in shock.
Ken Urker, the former fiancé of convicted murderer Gypsy Rose Blanchard, has died at the age of 33. Urker was discovered unresponsive in Louisiana, TMZ reports
Family sources told the publication that Urker was discovered at home. He and Blanchard shared a 21-month-old daughter that they welcomed in December 2024
Urker's sister, Autumn, reportedly confirmed his death on Thursday night after going live on TikTok.
She said her brother's last words to her had been, 'I love you.'
The Daily Mail has reached out to Blanchard's representatives for comment.
The former couple shared a 21-month-old daughter , Aurora Raina Urker, whom they welcomed on December 28, 2024.
Her birth coincided with the one-year anniversary of Blanchard's release from prison after she served seven years behind bars for her part in the murder of her abusive mother, Claudine 'Dee Dee' Blanchard.
Blanchard and Urker had an on–off relationship as they got engaged in October 2018 while she was incarcerated, only for them to split months later, before reuniting in August 2019.
After they separated again for several years, she went on to tie the knot with another man, Ryan Scott Anderson, in July 2022, while she was still serving time for killing her mother.
In March 2024, three months after her release, Blanchard announced that she and Anderson had separated, and in April of that year, she and Urker reconciled.

Blanchard was a victim as a child of Munchausen's syndrome by proxy, after her mother Dee Dee forced her to pose as an invalid by remaining in a wheelchair at all times in public.
Dee Dee shaved Gypsy-Rose's head and kept her drugged to convince the world that her daughter had muscular dystrophy and was battling leukemia.
But their warped relationship came to an end in 2015, when Gypsy-Rose's boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, crept into their home in Springfield, Missouri, and stabbed Dee Dee to death. She was 48.
Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and spent nearly 10 years in prison before being released in December 2022 after being granted an early parole .
While in prison, she bonded with Urker after he sent her a letter, and they started corresponding.
Things soon turned romantic, and he went on to propose in 2018.
But after the Hulu miniseries The Act – which starred Joey King as Gypsy and Patricia Arquette as her mother – premiered a few months later and put an intense spotlight on Gypsy's story, she admitted in her memoir that Ken couldn't handle the sudden wave of attention.
After announcing her split from her husband, Ryan Anderson, in March 2024, Blanchard revealed in July of that year that she and her reunited fiancé Urker were expecting a child.

Following their reunion, Urker looked back on how they reconnected while speaking to People.
'The very first weekend of April [2024] is when I came to visit her for the first time after she had gotten out. We spent that weekend together and had an incredible time,' he said.
Their renewed connection was strong enough that they made plans to meet again a month later to attend a jazz festival together.
'Then shortly after that, we realized we were going to have a baby,' Urker added.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.title_zh: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.content_orig:
She appeared to still be breathing when witnesses were escorted out.
Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, is in critical condition at a hospital and receiving "life-saving care" after a botched execution attempt Wednesday night, her attorneys told reporters at an online press conference on Thursday.
"Christa is alive right now. We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care," said Randy Spivey, an attorney with the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender.
The legal team for Pike -- the first woman the state planned to execute in 200 years -- called on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence.
"The state of Tennessee has shown us again that they are not capable of carrying out an execution consistent with basic human dignity," Spivey said. "Last night was not just inefficient. It was cruel, and it was torturous."
"Ms. Pike was not just cooperative, but was trying to help instruct the people placing the IV lines of where she could they could find them," Spivey said. "She over and over again said, 'Please try up on my shoulder higher. Please try here. Please try here.'"
"That really was her biggest fear," Spivey added. "It was not a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death."
The governor has ordered a "third-party review" and a temporary halt to scheduled executions after the execution attempt.
"So far as we know, the Department of Correction followed exactly the protocol as outlined," the governor told reporters on Thursday. He said the state needs to know "why the outcome is different this time than ever before."
"There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn't have happened," Lee said.
"The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for," Lee said.
The governor said in an earlier statement that the "remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year."
Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., who is running for governor of Tennessee, spoke out about the botched execution attempt on social media Thursday, calling on the state to bring back the electric chair.
Witnesses to the execution said late Wednesday that authorities appeared to administer two rounds of lethal pentobarbitol but that the convicted murderer appeared to still be breathing an hour later when witnesses were escorted out of the chamber.
"I've witnessed five executions in Tennessee. Nothing about today was normal, typical -- at all," said reporter Tori Gessner with ABC Nashville affiliate WKRN, who was one of several journalists who witnessed the proceedings.
Multiple witnesses said they could hear Pike breathing and snoring very loudly after the drugs were administered, even after the curtains were closed on the execution chamber.
Glessner said when witnesses were escorted out at 8:53 p.m. local time, Pike was still heard snoring.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after being convicted of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Her attempted execution came after a series of last-minute legal challenges.
In an order issued earlier Wednesday, the U.S. Supreme Court, in a 6-3 decision, allowed Pike's execution to proceed, granting Tennessee's request to lift a lower court's stay of execution, allowing the state to proceed with the administration of Pike's death sentence before the warrant expired at midnight local time.
The court's majority did not explain its decision, which came hours after a federal appeals court paused the execution at the 11th hour to review the capital case. The state subsequently asked the U.S. Supreme Court to vacate the appeals court's stay.
The three liberal Supreme Court justices dissented to vacating the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit's stay of execution.
"The Court's decision to vacate that stay interferes with the Sixth Circuit's routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim," Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in the dissent, which was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson. "Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the State to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts. I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision."
In a 2-1 decision issued within two hours of the scheduled execution, Judge Jane Branstetter Stranch of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit wrote that a stay is necessary in the "interests of justice and the finality of Pike's impending execution" in order to review whether her allegations of sexual abuse and rape as a child were fully considered before Pike was sentenced to death. The execution was stayed "until further order of this court," the order stated.
In his dissenting opinion, Judge Richard Allen Griffin called the matter "another last-ditch meritless effort to delay a lawful execution."
In an application asking the Supreme Court to vacate the stay, Tennessee Department of Correction Warden Kenneth Nelsen argued that Pike is not likely to succeed because her claim was "already unsuccessfully presented." The state's "strong interest in finality and the surviving victims' right to closure" also require the high court to vacate the stay, he argued.
Members of the victim's family -- including her mother, stepfather and father -- planned to attend the execution, according to Nelsen's filing.
"It is far past time for Colleen's family to receive the closure they seek," the filing stated, asking the Supreme Court to vacate the stay of execution to "avoid rewarding Pike's abusive delay tactics" and "prevent further trauma to Colleen's family."
In a June court filing challenging her execution, Pike argued that due to her history of rape and sexual abuse, being "the lone female in a vulnerable position surrounded by male corrections officers during the last days of her life will trigger her PTSD and result in a torturous execution or mental decompensation to the point she will be incompetent to be executed."
The Tennessee Supreme Court rejected her claims. She subsequently filed an application for stay of execution, requesting that the U.S. Supreme Court review her claims alleging the method of execution would inflict cruel and unusual punishment because of her PTSD from childhood rapes and abuse. The Supreme Court denied that request on Tuesday.
Later that day, Pike filed a motion seeking to review her claim that her trial counsel provided ineffective assistance at sentencing and failed to introduce evidence of her history of child sexual abuse.
In a statement on the stay of execution, Pike's attorney, Stephen Ferrell with the Federal Defenders Services of Eastern Tennessee, said, "The court has stayed this recognizing the serious concerns about Christa's scheduled execution."
In 1996, Pike was found guilty of first-degree murder for beating, torturing and killing Slemmer, a fellow Jobs Corps worker from Knoxville, in a remote area of the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.
Pike, who was 18 when she committed the crime, had told a friend she planned to kill Slemmer because she "just felt mean that day" and admitted to committing the crime with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, according to court filings. Shipp was also convicted of first-degree murder for his role in the killing and sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole.
While incarcerated, Pike was convicted in 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in the assault on an inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
ABC News' Michael O'Keefe contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
articles.title_zh: Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
articles.content_orig:
Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general as a special prosecutor in investigating the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University.
The woman has alleged she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house. The case, which stems back to 2024, was reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
"New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it," Hochul said.
Hochul's announcement removes Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from overseeing the case.
The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office.
He has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten reopened the case after the civil lawsuit and said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.
"The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said in a statement.
The attorney general will, if warranted, prosecute any offences found by her investigation and present evidence to a grand jury, the governor said.
James, the state's chief legal officer, said on X that she stood ready "to lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
"The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James added.
Hochul and James are scheduled to provide an update on the investigation on Friday morning local time.
The woman at the centre of the case, identified anonymously as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.
She alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.
The case was initially referred to Van Houten, the top prosecutor in the county, in 2024.
Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.
This week, his office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.
Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has accused the district attorney of repeatedly changing his story amid news coverage of the case.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI fires three workers over mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.title_zh: OpenAI fires three workers over mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.
The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.
The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity has intensified in recent weeks.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," OpenAI's spokesperson said.
The BBC understands the former employees were not let go for raising safety concerns but for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.
Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.
OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites .
In an earlier incident an OpenAI system accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.
That incident led OpenAI to conduct a broad review of the activities of its AI models - called agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.
The AI lab said this week that it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its AI systems.
Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, OpenAI said.

In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic , called for AI development to slow down so its potential risks could be properly assessed.
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman have also called for measures to address concerns over AI.
On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI.
After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.

Professor Azeem Ibrahim says Russia’s heavily militarized Baltic enclave has become a testing ground for hybrid warfare targeting European infrastructure.
Russia’s warning that it could resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempts to isolate Kaliningrad is raising new concerns that the heavily militarized Russian exclave could become a flashpoint between Moscow and the alliance, as experts warn the territory is already being used to pressure Europe through hybrid warfare.
Moscow warned NATO in a diplomatic document that it was prepared to use "the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" if alliance members attempted to isolate Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia, Reuters reported Wednesday.
Kaliningrad, a Russian territory geographically separated from the Russian mainland, sits on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and hosts significant Russian military assets, including elements of Moscow’s Baltic Fleet.
RUSSIA THREATENS STRIKES ON UK MILITARY TARGETS, ‘CATASTROPHIC CONSEQUENCES’ OVER UKRAINE
Russian President Vladimir Putin looks on a map showing the Kaliningrad exclave and the rest of Russia, Sept. 10, 2006. (Konstantin Zavrazhin/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
The Russian document also raised the possibility of strikes against "decision-making centers" in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.
NATO rejected Moscow’s allegations in a response reviewed by Fox News Digital, saying the alliance is defensive and that none of its exercises or activities threaten Russian territory. The alliance also urged Russia to stop its "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Carrie Filipetti, executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, a nonpartisan network of foreign policy leaders, told Fox News Digital that Moscow has repeatedly used nuclear threats as a means of trying to deter Western support for Ukraine.
"Russia has threatened to use nuclear weapons in the past, including veiled references to tactical nuclear attacks at the beginning of Putin's invasion of Ukraine , lowering their formal threshold for launching a nuclear attack in 2024, placing Russia's nuclear forces on high alert, and restarting nuclear testing," Filipetti said. "It is very common for Putin to use these threats, because he sees it as a way to deter Europe and the United States from continuing to support Ukraine."
SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE. NOW EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS
The Blue Ridge-class command and control ship USS Mount Whitney participates in exercise Baltic Operations 2025 as ships sail in formation through the Baltic Sea, June 5, 2025. (U.S. Navy Courtesy Photo)
"The threat about a nuclear attack if Kaliningrad is threatened or isolated comes on the heels of a few developments," she added, pointing to NATO jets being scrambled over Russian aircraft, U.S. and NATO air drills near Kaliningrad last month, and heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Filipetti, who also served as a deputy assistant secretary at the State Department and as a senior policy advisor for the United States Mission to the United Nations (USUN), argued that the timing also reflects mounting pressure on Moscow as the war continues.
"Putin seems to understand that the tide is turning against him, and he's resorting to aggressive rhetoric to try to stop European support for Ukraine as he has tried to do in the past," she said.
Dr. Azeem Ibrahim, a research professor at the Strategic Studies Institute at the U.S. Army War College and chief strategy officer at the New Lines Institute, told Fox News Digital that NATO should take the warning seriously, particularly because of the broader role Kaliningrad is already playing in Moscow’s confrontation with Europe.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
NATO's largest annual maritime drill, Exercise Dynamic Mariner/Flotex 25, continues in the Gulf of Cadiz off southern Spain on March 28, 2025. (Burak Akbulut/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Ibrahim argued that while NATO has traditionally prepared for conventional military conflict involving "tanks and troops and divisions," Russia is increasingly using methods designed to disrupt the infrastructure and systems on which civilian societies depend.
"Russia is actually adopting a very different approach," he said, describing a strategy of hybrid warfare targeting "infrastructure" and "societies in general — what keeps societies functioning."
Ibrahim described Kaliningrad as the "front line" of that effort.
"It’s essentially become a Russian fortress," he said. "This is essentially a front-line operation of the Russians in terms of signals intelligence, signals interference and essentially mechanisms by which to carry out this hybrid warfare."
Such interference, Ibrahim said, could play a role in the broader confrontation by disrupting civilian communications and infrastructure before or alongside a conventional military attack.
"All of that would be preceded by interference operations like this to ensure that societies are not functioning, are not able to respond to emergency services, the news information services, etc.," Ibrahim said. "So governments lose control over what actually makes societies function."
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Soldiers from Poland’s 18th Division demonstrate battlefield medical training near the Belarus border after a serviceman from the division was killed in an attack by an illegal migrant. May 16, 2026. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
The challenge for NATO, he said, is that such operations can be more difficult to attribute than a conventional assault.
"Many times, you cannot trace exactly where a lot of this interference is actually coming from — attacks on power stations or internet and telecommunications, et cetera," Ibrahim said. "There’s always some sort of plausible deniability if it’s done by an actor who's very capable."
The ambiguity, Ibrahim argued, presents a challenge for an alliance built around collective defense against armed attack.
"NATO really does have to kind of reconfigure its posture to understand that these kinds of attacks are equivalent to essentially any sort of kinetic attack," he said.
Asked what NATO and neighboring Poland and Lithuania should do following Russia’s warning, Ibrahim called for the alliance to establish clearer consequences for hybrid attacks.
"We now need to start going on the offensive in terms of hybrid warfare and understanding the threat and pushing back and sending a very clear signal to Moscow that such threats will not stand," he said, arguing that a sufficiently serious hybrid attack should be considered capable of triggering NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense clause.
Lithuania, which directly borders Kaliningrad, rejected Moscow’s warning and accused Russia of trying to undermine NATO unity and Western support for Ukraine.
"Russia’s insinuations and threats have no basis. NATO is a defensive alliance and poses no threat to Russia or any other country," Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry told Fox News Digital. "Russia’s threatening is intended to fracture transatlantic unity and impede our support to Ukraine. Russia will not achieve its goals."
The ministry added: "We strongly condemn any threats to use force and irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. Russia must stop its aggression against Ukraine… Lithuania is strengthening its national defense system and capabilities, including air defense," the ministry said. "We train with our allies and work alongside NATO forces deployed in Lithuania. We are prepared to defend every inch of NATO territory and respond to any threats."
The ministry said Lithuania would also continue providing "comprehensive support to Ukraine and its fight against the aggressor Russia."

articles.title_zh: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.
UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.
Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes
"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."
However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.

articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Massachusetts man on charge of stalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote Thursday on X , referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He is alleged to have contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times in less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant is also accused of sending disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August-to-September time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
One message Proia is alleged to have written to Miller’s mother called Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message was said to feature a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia is alleged to have written, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, assistant director in charge the FBI’s Washington Field Office, told Bloomberg in a statement that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
What happened: Nike ( NKE ) stock fell as much as 6% in after-hours trading on Thursday after posting its fiscal first quarter results and announcing operational changes, which will include layoffs.
What's behind the move: Nike posted fiscal first quarter revenue of $11.21 billion, versus consensus estimates of $11.33 billion. That represented a 4% decline from the year-earlier period.
Earnings per share came in at $0.48, down from $0.49 a year ago.
The company said revenues are expected to decline in the high single digits in fiscal 2027. Nike's gross margin, however, expanded 60 basis points to 42.8%.
The company also announced operational changes in order to reduce costs and operate more efficiently.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," wrote CEO Elliott Hill in a letter to employees.
Decisions about impacted roles will begin in calendar year 2027 and beyond.
The results come nearly two years after Hill took the helm as CEO.
"This is a quarter you'd expect from a new CEO three or four quarters in, but not two years in," CFRA analyst Zach Warring, who has a Buy on the stock, told Yahoo Finance.
The analyst noted, "Valuations and expectations have been reset."
"Now they can kind of move forward and begin to return to growth, expand margins, and start to really work on some of the geographies that they're sluggish, which is obviously greater China and Europe," he added.
Read more: Caitlin Clark's new signature Nike shoe nearly sells out within first two hours of going on sale
What else you need to know: The company was already facing challenges when Hill took over. Nike had pulled back from several major retail partners as it sought to prioritize its own sales channels, giving competitors an opening to gain ground.
The turnaround has not been easy.
"We have more work to do in NIKE Sportswear, Jordan Brand and Greater China, and we're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses the right way for the long-term," Hill said in the company's earnings release.
In late August, Dick's Sporting Goods ( DKS ) offered up a brutal warning about its business, in part because Nike is heavily discounting slow-moving product.
Soccer icon Kylian Mbappé ended his long-term business tie-up with Nike last month and announced he will now be joining Swiss sports giant On ( ONON ).
Nike's stock recently dropped from the S&P 100 ( ^SP100 ) after nearly 20 years in the index.
Thursday's report is the first earnings release under new CFO Dave Denton, who previously held a role at Pfizer.

articles.title_orig: Judge blocks Trump's firing of top federal prosecutor in Seattle and restores him as U.S. attorney
articles.title_zh: Judge blocks Trump's firing of top federal prosecutor in Seattle and restores him as U.S. attorney
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A federal judge on Thursday blocked President Trump's firing of Roger Rogoff from his post as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, finding the president cannot unilaterally remove a U.S. attorney who has been tapped to the post by a district court.
U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian delivered his decision from the bench at the end of a hearing, during which he agreed to grant Rogoff's request to reinstate him until the Senate confirms a replacement. Mr. Trump nominated Simon Peter Serrano to the position of U.S. attorney in Seattle last month.
Bastian ruled that Rogoff is the U.S. attorney in the Western District of Washington and has been the "rightful holder of that office" since July 15, when the federal district judges in the region installed him to the role and he took his oath of office.
Mr. Trump fired Rogoff less than an hour after he was sworn in.
"The real issue to be decided in this case by this court appears to be one of first impression: can the president fire a U.S. attorney appointed by the district court?" Bastian said, later adding, "The answer to the question the court is faced with is no. The president cannot unilaterally fire a United States attorney appointed by the district court."
The Justice Department said it intends to appeal and will immediately seek to halt the ruling.
In addition to declaring Rogoff as the U.S. attorney, Bastian said Charles Neil Floyd, the first assistant who has been leading the office, "is not the United States attorney" for the Western District of Washington, and authority to perform the role's responsibilities was "improperly granted."
Mr. Trump signed an order last week that directed Floyd "to perform the functions and duties of the office of United States Attorney."
"Allowing the president to fire a U.S. attorney appointed by the district court would upend the framework created by the Constitution and the statutes, which together balance the president's right to appoint and the Senate's right to confirm," Bastian said. "Allowing the president to fire a United States attorney appointed by the court also eliminates the incentive to nominate a candidate that can be confirmed by the Senate. In other words, the executive and legislative branches are supposed to and encouraged to work together."
In his oral order, the judge prohibited the Trump administration from putting Rogoff's firing into effect until the U.S. attorney spot is filled by a Senate-confirmed candidate. He also said the administration cannot purport to remove Rogoff from his position, deny him access to benefits or resources of the position, or obstruct Rogoff from his ability to carry out his duties.
Finally, Bastian said the Trump administration cannot treat anyone other than Rogoff as U.S. attorney.
"The court finds it is in the public interest that the law be followed and that Mr. Rogoff take the office to which he has already taken the oath of office," he said.
"I care deeply about the rule of law and the careful checks and balances envisioned by our Founders and carried out by Congress," Rogoff said in a statement provided to CBS News. "I appreciate the judicial process and am now focused on assuming the role of U.S. attorney and getting to work for the people of Western Washington."
The U.S. attorney's office in Seattle has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since mid-2023. After Mr. Trump took office, he fired Tessa Gorman as the top prosecutor in the office. She had been serving temporarily before judges on the district court appointed her to the job in May 2024.
Floyd began leading the office as interim U.S. attorney in October, but his appointment was subject to a 120-day clock, which expired in February. He then began serving as first assistant U.S. attorney, the second-in-command, and said at the time that he would continue leading the office.
Because Mr. Trump had not by that time put forth a nominee to serve as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, the district judges exercised their authority under a federal law governing U.S. attorney vacancies to tap Rogoff for the job. That law allows the attorney general to appoint an interim U.S. attorney, who is subject to a 120-day term. Once that appointment expires, the district court can either agree to extend that prosecutor's tenure or appoint its own U.S. attorney until the Senate confirms a replacement.
Following his swift firing, Rogoff filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration and argued that his removal was unlawful. He argued that if not blocked by the court, the Trump administration's "actions will permit the Executive Branch to evade the Senate's advice-and-consent role indefinitely."
Mr. Trump has attempted to install his preferred candidates for U.S. attorney in several other places, including Nevada, New York, Virginia and New Jersey. Federal courts have in those instances, some of which involve a slightly different mechanism, found the appointments unlawful.
Rogoff, however, appears to be the first ousted prosecutor to challenge his firing in court.

China’s major refiners have suspended most refined fuel exports for October as Beijing prioritizes domestic supply security, removing another source of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel from an already severely constrained global market.
PetroChina has cancelled several gasoline and jet fuel cargoes scheduled for October, while Zhejiang Petrochemical did not schedule exports during China’s week-long National Day holiday, Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the matter. Beijing has yet to authorize October exports outside Hong Kong and Macau, although shipments could resume after the holiday ends on October 7 depending on domestic inventories and refinery output.
The move follows a sharp deterioration in China’s own fuel-stock position. Kpler estimates commercial diesel and gasoil inventories are around 20 million barrels below pre-war levels, while gasoline stocks are roughly 9 million barrels short of the threshold Beijing wants restored before allowing exports to normalize.
China had significantly increased exports during the summer. Official customs data showed total oil-product exports reached 6.01 million tonnes in August, up 12.7% year-on-year and the highest since March 2024, according to S&P Global. At the time, Chinese refiners said Beijing had not yet restricted clean-product exports despite tightening domestic supply.
The reversal comes as global diesel supplies are already being squeezed by Middle Eastern disruptions and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. S&P Global warned this week that Asian fuel markets have limited surplus supply, meaning any further restriction on U.S. diesel exports would increase competition for Asian and Middle Eastern barrels.
China’s own government has meanwhile intervened to limit the domestic impact of high international oil prices, partially suppressing scheduled gasoline and diesel price increases in September while instructing refiners to ensure stable supplies.

But instead of their prey, they would be met by host Chris Hansen (played by Robert Pattinson), who would interrogate the predators about why they were pursuing illicit and illegal affairs. The suspects were then arrested by law enforcement waiting outside the house.
The film is based more specifically on the 2009 Esquire article “Tonight on ‘Dateline’ This Man Will Die,” which chronicled an episode of the show involving Louis William Conradt Jr., an assistant district attorney in Murphy, Texas, who died by suicide after being caught in a police sting conducted in coordination with the “Predator” team.
Hansen is continuing his work on his media platform, TruBlu , which hosts shows such as the spiritual successor to “Predator,” “Takedown With Chris Hansen,” which launched in 2022.
Variety spoke with Hansen a few days after he watched “Primetime.” He discussed his perspective on its box office success, which parts are most upsetting to his former colleagues and what legal action he might take against A24.

articles.title_orig: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.title_zh: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, from left; father Tim Ganger, mother Donna Ganger, brother Luke Ganger and brother Brent Ganger, listen during a news conference after the family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
The family of Renee Good , the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.
One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.
It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."
In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges , including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."
Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.
According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.
"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."
Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."
The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.
The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges . DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.
A memorial for Renee Good, who was killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, remains in place at the site of her death, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."
At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.
"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."
Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."

articles.title_orig: Lindsay Clancy judge denies motion to force not guilty finding - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Lindsay Clancy judge denies motion to force not guilty finding - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
A judge on Thursday denied Lindsay Clancy ’s attempt to throw out her triple-murder case based on a purported lack of evidence -- putting her one step closer to a potential retrial.
Judge William Sullivan denied the motion for a required finding of not guilty in a five-page written order, concluding that prosecutors presented enough evidence to “permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder.”
The ruling comes two days after the first hearing in the case since a mistrial was declared on Sept. 4 after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
While Clancy did not contest that she killed her children during the trial, her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, said in Tuesday’s hearing that the case should be thrown out because prosecutors failed to prove she was responsible for her children's deaths, in addition to continuing to argue her insanity defense.
Sullivan rejected both arguments in his ruling Thursday.
“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder,” he wrote.
Clancy’s second motion to dismiss the case -- which argues that retrying the case would amount to double jeopardy -- is still pending.
Clancy pleaded not guilty to three murder charges in the deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson, and infant son Callan, who were strangled at the family's home in Duxbury, a Boston suburb, on Jan. 24, 2023.
The former nurse attempted suicide on the night of her children's deaths, leaving her paralyzed and in a wheelchair.
During Clancy's five-week trial, Reddington argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis -- considered a psychiatric emergency, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists -- and was overmedicated when she strangled her children and attempted to take her own life.
Prosecutors argued that Clancy was criminally responsible for her children's deaths and was capable of understanding the severity of her actions.
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters Tuesday that his office is still evaluating whether to retry Clancy, saying a decision would be made "as soon as we get all the information that we can."
The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Nov. 2.

articles.title_orig: Trump sends third aircraft carrier to Middle East with 10K more troops — as he weighs post-midterm Iran assault
articles.title_zh: Trump sends third aircraft carrier to Middle East with 10K more troops — as he weighs post-midterm Iran assault
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON —The Pentagon is dispatching a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as President Trump is reportedly weighing whether to ramp up the war against Iran after the midterms.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt and its strike group departed San Diego on Sunday, carrying up to 9,000 to 10,000 service members as Trump mulls over his next steps with Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported . The strike group is reportedly slated to arrive in November.
It’s not immediately clear if the deployment is intended to relieve another aircraft carrier in the region or add to the force posture there.
Already, the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington are stationed in the region, the latter of which relieved the USS Abraham Lincoln in August after its record-setting long deployment and allegedly bleak conditions for its crew. The USS George Washington is typically deployed in the Pacific Ocean and is ported in Japan.
Due to harrowing reports of weary sailors attempting to jump overboard amid shortages of critical supplies thanks to Iranian strikes that disrupted supply lines in the region, particularly a key port in Bahrain, the Pentagon made plans for the USS Theodore Roosevelt to be ready for a long stay.
This included maximizing its stash of food, hygiene, retail, and other critical supplies before its deployment, something Navy leadership touted last month .
They also took steps to ensure sailors will have more reliable communication with their families back at home and better quality of life amenities aboard the aircraft carrier.
“That means new entertainment equipment on the mess decks, more durable fitness equipment, spare cardio machines ready for our placement, and even holiday materials purchased ahead of time,” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said in a video announcement last motth about the reforms made.
The Post contacted the Pentagon and US Central Command for comment.
Last week, Trump rejected Iran’s proposed seven-day cease-fire offer , calling it unacceptable. Iran indicated it would open up the Strait of Hormuz during that time, but top administration officials have contended that the US is already getting oil through the critical chokepoint.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
There are believed to be around 20 Navy ships in the region helping with escort
The president also indicated that he may resume a bombing campaign against Iran after the midterm elections.
“Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world,” he told Time magazine . “With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”
For weeks, the Trump administration has maintained a blockade around Iran as part of a brutal economic pressure campaign. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also spearheaded Operation Economic Outcast to pressure other countries to cease business with Iran.

articles.title_orig: As Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level Since 2023, Buyers Look at ARMs
articles.title_zh: As Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level Since 2023, Buyers Look at ARMs
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates keep going up.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% this week, up from 7.03% last week, according to Freddie Mac data released Thursday. Mortgage rates have risen for six straight weeks, and this week brought the biggest one-week jump in nearly four years. Rates are now at their highest level since November 2023.
Turmoil in the bond market is driving rates higher. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen in recent months as investors worry that the Iran war and increased government spending could further stoke inflation and push the Federal Reserve toward higher rates for longer.
If you’re currently in the market for a home, the good news is you may be facing less competition from rate-sensitive buyers who are stepping back. But if you need a mortgage, the bad news is you will likely pay more in monthly costs than you would have just a few months ago.
But even with borrowing costs high – and potentially headed higher – a sub-7% mortgage rate may still be within reach for some buyers. The trade-off could be a riskier loan or a much bigger upfront payment.
Most home buyers opt for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage because it typically offers lower monthly payments and predictable costs.
But it’s not the only option. Other types of mortgages may offer lower interest rates, potentially saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.
A 15-year mortgage typically has a lower interest rate than a 30-year mortgage, though monthly payments are significantly higher. Another option that is becoming increasingly popular lately: adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs).
As of the latest data last week, “ARM loans, with rates around 80 basis points lower than fixed rate loans, accounted for 10.3% of applications, the highest share since October 2025,” according to Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
How are higher interest rates and rising prices affecting you?
But ARM loans, the mortgage products that helped fuel housing market risk in the lead-up to the 2008 financial crisis, are riskier than fixed-rate loans . They typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can be hit with sharply higher monthly payments.
“It may work well for some borrowers who are expecting to move or refinance in four or five years,” said Jeremy Luke, a divisional director at Chase Home Lending. “It may not work for all.”
Another way to get a lower mortgage rate is to take over someone’s existing mortgage as an assumable loan .
Not all home loans can be passed to a home buyer, but most government-backed loans, such as those from the Federal Housing Administration, the US Department of Veterans Affairs and the US Department of Agriculture, are assumable.
However, the approval process for an assumable mortgage can take longer. And because the buyer takes over only the seller’s remaining loan balance, they may need to bring significantly more cash to the table to cover the difference between that balance and the home’s purchase price.
The rate an individual buyer gets depends on more than market conditions. Lenders also consider factors such as the borrower’s credit score, debt-to-income ratio and down payment, said Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot.
After shopping around, if you are unsatisfied with the rates you’ve been offered, it’s often possible to pay more up front in exchange for a reduced interest rate.
Permanent buydowns lower your interest rate for the life of the loan, whereas temporary buydowns, which can be cheaper, lower your rate for only the first few years.
But it’s important not to overdo it, DerGurahian said.
“You don’t want to put so much money down that you can’t do what you need to do to live in your house and live day-to-day,” he said.
Sometimes, the home’s seller or a builder can cover the cost of a rate buydown.
Builders are leaning more heavily on incentives to attract buyers to new construction, offering concessions such as mortgage rate buydowns and closing-cost credits. In September, 66% of builders reported using sales incentives, up from 63% in August and the highest share since December, according to the National Association of Home Builders’ sentiment survey.
A buyer should also understand the demand picture in their local market, said DerGurahian.
If it’s a buyer’s market, that means the supply of homes in that area exceeds demand, giving home buyers the upper hand. If a homeowner is motivated to sell, they may be willing to offer concessions to attract a buyer. If sellers have the upper hand in a local market, though, it’s less likely.
Certain buyers may have access to federal programs that can help them secure more favorable mortgage rates, including VA loans for eligible veterans and USDA loans for buyers purchasing homes in qualifying rural areas.
There are also banks and credit unions that offer relationship pricing or preferential rates.
For example, Chase occasionally runs “rate sales” where home buyers (and homeowners looking to refinance) can lock in discounted rates, Luke said.
Some banks, including Chase, also offer a discounted rate if customers move eligible deposits and investments into that bank, Luke added.
It pays to shop around. Experts generally recommend applying with at least three different mortgage lenders to make sure you’re getting a competitive rate. Compare the rates offered, closing costs and other fees to get a clearer picture of the total cost of each loan.
And you don’t necessarily have to worry about multiple credit checks dinging your score. To shop around for mortgages without hurting your credit, limit your search to a window of 14 to 45 days, according to Bankrate.

articles.title_orig: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.title_zh: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.content_orig:
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The disgraced hip-hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.
They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which include video of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.
“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.
TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.
Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.
“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.
Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.
“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.
Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or gray sweatpants and shirts.
Meals are delivered in trays, but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.
“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.
It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.
He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.
The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)
“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.
Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein .
Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a “new performance tier of AI upscaling” that’s a result of Sony’s Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post .
Sony says that PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on the PS5 Pro , “remains the gold standard,” and in Digital Foundry ’s early hands-on with the tech , it does seem that QSSR isn’t as fast as PSSR because the PS5 doesn’t have dedicated machine learning silicon. As a result, you should probably expect closer to an upscaled 1440p resolution on PS5 instead of the upscaled 4K on PS5 Pro.
”On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it,” Sony principal graphics R&D engineer Daniel Craig told Digital Foundry . “On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode.”
But Craig also said that QSSR is “fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR” after only a few days of tuning, making it likelier that PS5 developers will take advantage. The tech will be “offered broadly to all PlayStation developers,” Sony says.
Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first games to take advantage of QSSR, and are getting patches today to offer the tech as “an additional graphics option on PS5.” ( Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition also launches today .) Here are a couple videos from Sony showing off how QSSR looks in those games, and it appears to make graphics a little bit sharper:
Digital Foundry writes that “the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference.”

articles.title_orig: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific causing military rescue mission
articles.title_zh: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific causing military rescue mission
articles.content_orig:
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.
Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.
"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.
Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.
"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.
Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.
"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.
"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.
At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.
"We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.
The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release , which included images of the rescue.
French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.
"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.
Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.
The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.
Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.
In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.
The New Zealand military released dramatic drone video of the yacht plunging below the water's surface and the crew ultimately being rescued.
A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.
Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.
But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.
"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."
Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.
"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."
Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.
The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board.  Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

articles.title_zh: Exclusive | David Ellison Asks CNN CEO to Stay After Paramount-Warner Deal Closes
articles.content_orig:
By Ted Johnson , Jill Goldsmith
Paramount CEO David Ellison wants CEO Mark Thompson to remain at CNN after the Warner Bros Discovery deal closes, a move that would settle at least some of the speculation over the future of the network under its incoming new owners.
Talks between Ellison and Thompson are said to be in their early stages, according to sources familiar with the matter. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Ellison’s plans to retain Thompson, who was tapped to lead the network in 2023 . Since then, he has sought to integrate the linear and digital operations while launching CNN’s All Access subscription and streaming service.
Under Thompson, CNN also has continued to aggressively report on the Trump administration, while embarking on a lawsuit against the president after he banned the network and two other outlets from the White House grounds. The network also has defended its reporters in the face of attacks by the president, including its chief White House correspondent, Kaitlan Collins.
Thompson was president and CEO of the New York Times Company from 2012-20, after serving as director-general of the BBC for eight years.
RELATED: CNN CEO Mark Thompson Addresses Donald Trump’s White House Ban, Pending Paramount Merger In Town Hall
The Journal also reported that Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News, is not expected to have a role in CNN. There has been speculation among current and former staffers at the network that Weiss could be given additional responsibilities after the deal close, as CBS News and CNN will become sister networks.
According to a financial filing earlier this year, CNN was expected to generate $1.8 billion in revenue for the 2026 fiscal year and $600 million in profit. The network was estimated to reach $2.2 billion in revenue in 2030, with $700 million in profit.

articles.title_orig: Winner of Nikon microscopy photo contest faces criticism over AI usage
articles.title_zh: Winner of Nikon microscopy photo contest faces criticism over AI usage
articles.content_orig:
The organizers of a highly regarded scientific photography contest are reviewing this year’s winning entry following criticism over the use of AI.
Nikon has announced that it’s “carefully re-reviewing the information” provided by Ning Xu, whose short video of intricate cell movement won the annual Small World In Motion competition in September.
At the time, Xu was a researcher at Tsinghua University in China. He’s since joined National University of Singapore as a research fellow, according to Nikon .
In a post on LinkedIn on Saturday, Nikon said that, “Xu is respectfully complying and has provided detailed technical documentation outlining the microscopy equipment, imaging methods, and processing techniques used to create the source video.”
Astonishing footage of abnormal cell movement in lungs wins 2026 Nikon video microscopy prize
The video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder, Nikon said at the time the winner was revealed.
In mid-September, Nikon announced that the video, which was created using an advanced microscopic imaging tool, had won the 16th annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition.
Last week, the competition posted the video on LinkedIn, where it received a number of critical comments from other users.
Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, said there were “many serious problems with this video.” He said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added.
Ian Donovan, a PhD student at UT Southwestern Medical Center, wrote that the video has “an embedded SynthID watermark identifying synthetic/AI-generated content.”
Xu replied to some of the criticism on Nikon’s LinkedIn post, saying that “AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
“It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added.
“A more detailed description of the optical system and quantitative analysis of the ciliary motion are currently being prepared for publication, and we hope to make these available soon,” he said.
“For me, the important distinction is between using an image to make a scientific claim and using visualization to communicate the beauty of scientific data,” added Xu. “Both can have a place, as long as we are clear about which is which.”
CNN has contacted competition organizers for comment.
CNN has tried contacting Xu for comment directly and via the Tsinghua University and the National University of Singapore.
